claim: Sherman and Turk-Browne, 2020 found that stimuli that trigger strong predictions are encoded less well.
source: In addition to surprise, recent work by Sherman and Turk-Browne, 2020 suggests that predictive certainty may play a role in shaping encoding policy: They found that stimuli that trigger strong predictions (i.e., high certainty about upcoming events) are encoded less well.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Bonasia et al., 2018 found that events that were more typical were associated with lower levels of medial temporal lobe (MTL) activation during episodic encoding.
source: In keeping with this point, Bonasia et al., 2018 found that, during episodic encoding, events that were more typical (and thus were associated with more predictive certainty, and less surprise) were associated with lower levels of medial temporal lobe (MTL) activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: It makes sense to focus episodic encoding on time periods where there is high surprise and low predictive certainty.
source: Intuitively, it makes sense to focus episodic encoding on time periods where there is high surprise and low predictive certainty
evidence: This claim is based on inference about optimal encoding strategies.

claim: If events in a sequence are unsurprising and associated with high predictive certainty, existing neocortical schemas are sufficient to reconstruct that event, and no new learning is necessary.
source: if events in a sequence are unsurprising and associated with high predictive certainty, this means that existing (neocortical) schemas are sufficient to reconstruct that event, and no new learning is necessary (or, if learning is required, it is possible that neocortex could handle this 'schema-consistent' learning on its own; McClelland, 2013; McClelland et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on inference with citations to relevant theoretical work.

claim: If events in a sequence do not follow a schema or violate that schema, the only way to predict those events later will be to store them in episodic memory.
source: Conversely, if events in a sequence do not follow a schema (leading to uncertainty) or violate that schema (leading to surprise), the only way to predict those events later will be to store them in episodic memory.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about when episodic encoding is necessary.

claim: The model stores each episodic memory as a distinct entity, and old memories are never overwritten or updated.
source: Another major simplification in the model's encoding policy is that it stores each episodic memory as a distinct entity (see Figure 1B). Old memories are never overwritten or updated.
evidence: This claim describes a property of the model's encoding mechanism.

claim: A growing literature on memory reconsolidation suggests that memory reminders can result in participants accessing an existing memory and then updating that memory, rather than forming a new memory outright.
source: However, a growing literature on memory reconsolidation suggests that memory reminders can result in participants accessing an existing memory and then updating that memory, rather than forming a new memory outright (Dudai and Eisenberg, 2004; Dudai, 2009; Hardt et al., 2010; Wang and Morris, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to literature on memory reconsolidation.

claim: The model could implement memory updating by having it try to retrieve before it encodes a new memory; if it succeeds in retrieving a stored memory above a certain threshold, it could update that memory rather than creating a new memory.

evidence: This claim is a speculation about benefits of model extensions with citations to relevant neural data.

evidence: This claim describes a limitation of the current model.

source: Including more detailed circuit-level mechanisms would allow us to leverage the wealth of data that exist at this level to constrain the model.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about benefits of adding more biological detail.

source: For example, work by Hasselmo and colleagues has shown how cholinergic projections from the basal forebrain to the hippocampus can shift hippocampal dynamics between encoding and retrieval based on whether the retrieval cue is novel or familiar (Hasselmo et al., 1995; Hasselmo et al., 1996; Hasselmo and Wyble, 1997)

evidence: This claim explains the rationale for the current model design.

source: Also, natural events unfold over multiple timescales.

evidence: This claim explains the rationale for the current simulation design.

evidence: This claim describes planned future work with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The policies explored in this paper do not encompass the full range of ways in which the use of episodic memory can be optimized.

claim: In addition to questions about when to encode and retrieve, one can consider optimizations of what is stored in memory and how memory is cued.

evidence: This claim is based on general knowledge about memory optimization strategies.

claim: Mnemonic techniques like the method of loci involve considerable recoding of to-be-learned information and structured cuing strategies.
source: These kinds of optimizations are evident in mnemonic techniques like the method of loci (Yates, 1966), which involve considerable recoding of to-be-learned information (to maximize distinctiveness of stored memories) and also structured cuing strategies (to ensure that these distinctive memory traces can be found after they are stored).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to work on mnemonic techniques.

claim: The kinds of policies explored in this paper fall more on the 'automatic' end of the spectrum.
source: We think that the kinds of policies explored in this paper (e.g., retrieving more when uncertain, encoding more at the end of an event) fall more on the 'automatic' end of the spectrum
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the nature of the policies studied.

claim: The policies explored in this paper require no special training and are deployed even in incidental learning situations.
source: as evidenced by the fact that they require no special training and are deployed even in incidental learning situations (e.g., while people are watching a movie, without specifically trying to remember it; Chen et al., 2016; Baldassano et al., 2017).

claim: The 'simple' policies discussed in the paper and more complex strategies like method of loci fall on a continuum.
source: However, we think that it is best to view our 'simple' policies and more complex strategies as falling on a continuum.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the relationship between different types of memory strategies.

claim: While the policies discussed may be deployed automatically in adults, the simulations show that at least some of these policies can be learned through experience.
source: While the policies we discuss may be deployed automatically in adults, our simulations show that at least some of these policies (e.g., modulating episodic retrieval based on predictive certainty) can be learned through experience
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the simulation results.

claim: The policies discussed might not yet be automatic in young children.
source: and indeed these strategies might not (yet) be automatic in young children.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about developmental differences.

claim: In principle, there is nothing stopping a model like this from learning more elaborate strategies given the right kinds of experience and a rich enough action space.
source: Furthermore, in principle, there is nothing stopping a model like ours from learning more elaborate strategies given the right kinds of experience and a rich enough action space.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the potential capabilities of the model.

claim: Most memory-augmented neural networks used in machine learning encode at each time point.
source: For example, most memory-augmented neural networks used in machine learning encode at each time point (Graves et al., 2014; Graves et al., 2016; Ritter et al., 2018; Pritzel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claim: The results provide initial evidence that taking episodic 'snapshots' too frequently can actually harm performance.
source: Our results provide initial evidence that taking episodic 'snapshots' too frequently can actually harm performance.
evidence: This claim is based on the simulation results on encoding policies.

claim: Selective encoding and retrieval policies will be most useful when there is a substantial risk of recalling lure memories that lead to incorrect predictions, and a substantial cost associated with making these incorrect predictions.
source: Based on our simulations, we expect that these selective policies will be most useful when there is a substantial risk of recalling lure memories that lead to incorrect predictions, and a substantial cost associated with making these incorrect predictions.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on inference from the simulation results.

claim: The modeling work builds on research showing that episodic memory is a resource that the brain can flexibly draw upon to solve tasks.
source: The modeling work presented here builds on a wide range of research showing that episodic memory is a resource that the brain can flexibly draw upon to solve tasks (see, e.g., Shohamy and Turk-Browne, 2013; Palombo et al., 2019; Palombo et al., 2015; Bakkour et al., 2019; Biderman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to relevant research.

claim: In addition to studying episodic memory using tasks that probe this system in isolation, it is valuable to study how episodic memory is used in more complex situations, in concert with working memory and semantic memory.
source: This view implies that, in addition to studying episodic memory using tasks that probe this system in isolation, it is also valuable to study how episodic memory is used in more complex situations, in concert with working memory and semantic memory, to solve tasks and make predictions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the implications of the flexible memory view.

claim: The authors have leveraged advances in AI that make it possible for models to learn how to use episodic memory.
source: To engage with findings of these sort, we have leveraged advances in AI that make it possible for models to learn how to use episodic memory
evidence: This claim describes the methodological approach of the work.

claim: The simulations provide a way of predicting how episodic memory should be deployed to obtain rewards, as a function of the properties of the learning environment.
source: our simulations provide a way of predicting how episodic memory should be deployed to obtain rewards, as a function of the properties of the learning environment.
evidence: This claim describes the contribution of the modeling work.

claim: The model can spur a virtuous cycle of predictions, experiments, and model revision that will bring us to a richer understanding of how the brain uses episodic memory.
source: our hope is that this model (and others like it, such as the model by Ritter et al., 2018) can spur a virtuous cycle of predictions, experiments, and model revision that will bring us to a richer understanding of how the brain uses episodic memory.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the potential impact of the work.

claim: Episodic retrieval in the model is content-based.
source: Episodic retrieval in our model is content-based.
evidence: This claim describes a property of the model's retrieval mechanism.

claim: The retrieval process returns a weighted average of all episodic memories, where the weight of each memory is equal to its activation.
source: The retrieval process returns a weighted average of all episodic memories, where the weight of each memory is equal to its activation
evidence: This claim describes the computational mechanism of retrieval.

claim: The evidence for a given episodic memory is the cosine similarity between that memory and the current neocortical pattern.
source: The evidence for a given episodic memory is the cosine similarity between that memory and the current neocortical pattern (the cell state of the LSTM).
evidence: This claim describes how evidence is computed in the model.

claim: Memories that are similar to the current neocortical pattern will have a larger influence on the pattern that gets reinstated.
source: Hence, memories that are similar to the current neocortical pattern will have a larger influence on the pattern that gets reinstated.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the retrieval mechanism.

claim: The evidence accumulation process is governed by the episodic memory gate (EM gate) and the level of competition across memories.
source: The evidence accumulation process is governed by the episodic memory gate (EM gate) and the level of competition across memories (Figure 1C), which are stored separately from each other (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim describes the parameters controlling retrieval as shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The EM gate is controlled by the neocortical network.
source: The EM gate is controlled by the neocortical network (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This claim describes the control mechanism for the EM gate as shown in Figures 1A and 1C.

claim: A higher EM gate value increases the activation of all memories, and setting the EM gate value to zero turns off episodic retrieval completely.
source: The EM gate, in turn, controls whether episodic retrieval happens – a higher EM gate value increases the activation of all memories, and setting the EM gate value to zero turns off episodic retrieval completely
evidence: This claim describes the functional role of the EM gate.

claim: The level of competition adjusts the contrast of activations across all memories.
source: The level of competition (i.e., lateral inhibition) adjusts the contrast of activations across all memories
evidence: This claim describes the functional role of the competition parameter.

claim: Making the level of competition higher or lower interpolates between one-winner-take-all recall versus recalling an average of multiple memories.
source: making the level of competition higher or lower interpolates between one-winner-take-all recall versus recalling an average of multiple memories.
evidence: This claim describes the effect of varying the competition parameter.

claim: In all simulations, the level of competition was set to be well above zero (0.8).
source: In all of our simulations, we set the level of competition to be well above zero (0.8, to be exact)
evidence: This claim describes a parameter setting used in the simulations.

claim: There is overwhelming evidence that episodic retrieval is competitive.
source: given the overwhelming evidence that episodic retrieval is competitive (Anderson and Reder, 1999; Norman and O'Reilly, 2003; Norman, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on competitive retrieval.

claim: The model uses a neural network that learns to control the level of the EM gate value, instead of optimizing the LCA parameters to fit empirical results.
source: Note that, instead of optimizing the LCA parameters to fit empirical results (e.g., as in the work by Polyn et al., 2009), we use a neural network that learns to control the level of the EM gate value.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological choice in the model design.

claim: The model's goal is to maximize reward by making correct predictions and avoiding incorrect predictions.
source: As described below, in the Model training and testing section, the model's goal is to maximize reward by making correct predictions and avoiding incorrect predictions
evidence: This claim describes the objective function for the model.
